utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber is not informed about any preliminaries. Therefore could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. While the witness is coming in, I just wanted to let the Chamber know that in respect of 65 ter 9389, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is -- yes, is that P306.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think it's P2 -- P296. This is the -- the letter with the reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I was able to locate General Mladic's letter to General Nambiar. I provided that to the Defence. They have a copy of it. What I propose to do, Mr. President, is to tender that document separately because this 9389 was an associated exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: But I think I would like to tender that for the completion of the record and for the Chamber's benefit, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so that we have the complete information, yes. Has it been uploaded already?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It has been uploaded and we've assigned it 65 ter number 28451, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll deal with it in -- later today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Abdel-Razek.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Abdel-Razek, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Petrusic. And before we start, Mr. Abdel-Razek, may I urge you to focus your answers very much and very precisely to the question that is put to you. If we need more background information about the matters you are telling us about, Mr. Petrusic will ask you for it. Please proceed, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, sir, yesterday you said that UNPROFOR maps were in your office with the disposition of forces of the Bosnian and Serb forces. Is my understanding correct? Just tell me whether what I'm saying is right or wrong.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Were the artillery firing positions marked on these maps as well, either of the Muslim or the Serb army? Again, just please give a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: During your mandate, during your mission there, was it possible to tour the positions of both armies, their lines of fire, as it were?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I didn't hear the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You hear the translation, then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For listening to the questions, Mr. Abdel-Razek should be on the English channel, or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that we have translation in both directions now. Mr. Abdel-Razek, do you hear the question in your own language, or do you hear it in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I prefer to listen to them in Arabic. I prefer to listen to them in Arabic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then is the witness on the right channel to receive the Arabic? What channel is that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's channel 7, and it was set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's continue. Everything has been set, Mr. Abdel-Razek, for you to receive the question in Arabic. If it doesn't work, please let me know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, did your mission imply that you could tour the positions both of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the army of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not tour these positions in persons -- in person. However, I visited some Serbian positions. When Mr. Goulding visited us in the sector, we also visited some artillery positions in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you've given a partial answer to my question, but I ask you kindly to focus on the question itself. What about your mission itself? Did it envisage that you could do that? Just tell me whether this was envisaged within the terms of your mission or not.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I was the commander of the sector. There were also the observers and many other units deployed. The commander of the sector did not have the possibility to tour these areas freely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... that is not the question that is put to you. The question that is put to you is that whether your mission, not you as a commander, but whether those subordinated to you in your mission, whether they will -- whether they were able to tour the positions also on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir. International observers were present in areas facing the Serbian positions and the positions belonging to the Bosnian government. However, we had 11 posts were on the Serbian side and 3 posts on the government side. We used to call them Baba or Lima or something like that. So these people were in charge of observing, of assessing the direction of the fire, and to notify us in the command. However, when one of the UN officials visited the sector, I went with him and we checked on some Serbian positions, and we visited one artillery post as you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, now I'd like to move on to paragraph 77 of your statement. That is where you speak of mobile vehicles where mortars were mounted. From time to time, they would fire shells, and that happened once from an area close to your command. This is what I'd be interested in. We are speaking in general terms now, in terms of principle. If mortar shells were fired from these vehicles, did the other side have the right to respond to this kind of artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, this is asking for legal opinion, isn't it? I will not -- you could ask the witness what his understanding was of whether they were entitled to respond.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer? Everyone knew that the United Nations, all the posts belonging to the United Nations, do not entitle any warring factions -- I rephrase it. According to the UN, warring factions could not operate in an a perimeter of 500 metres from the UN posts, be it mobile posts or the fixed posts such as the Tito Barracks, the airport, or the PTT building. It was forbidden for anyone to get closer than 500 metres from these UN posts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. That was not the question. The question was that if mortars were fired from movable vehicles, whether the party who received those shells incoming, whether in your view they were entitled to respond to that fire.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a military commander, I say yes, they had the right to retaliate. However, they should have taken into account the fact that retaliation might target some UN building, and this is what happened. This is what was important for us. The vehicles equipped with mortars and shelling from UN proximity, from UN buildings' proximity would then jeopardise the safety of the UN buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Abdel-Razek, the question did not include the element you add that it is that it was -- that fire was -- that there was fire from the proximity of UN premises or that the return fire would go into that direction. The question was put in very general terms: If from wherever in Sarajevo mortars were fired from these vehicles, whether the party receiving that fire was entitled to return that fire. So let's just do as if there was no UN even. Let's just imagine, because the UN is not the issue raised by Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I said that the unit that is targeted by the shells is entitled to retaliate. This is from a military point of view. However, we are talking about a city that was hosting UN posts and also a city where civilians were living. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The last part that civilians were living there, that apparently is for you also a relevant factor to consider when responding fire. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, these vehicles with mobile mortars, could they also be found near other facilities, civilian facilities? I'm primarily referring to hospitals, schools, and the like. Post offices.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you know that during your tour there shells were fired from these vehicles, from the proximity of some other facilities?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I mentioned this to Mr. Galic. Ganic and not Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Today, to the best of your recollection, General, can you tell us what these locations were?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: During our tour, we saw some locations close to the PTT building, and the district, and the main hospital. So close to the PTT building, district and main hospital. This is what I saw during my tour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you are saying that from these locations a mobile vehicle with a mortar mounted on it fired from there and the Serbs responded by firing at these locations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I meant. They used to fire from these locations, and they used to receive retaliation firing from the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you mentioned your meeting with a high official of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Ejub Ganic. You lodged a protest with him. Am I correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I lodged a protest with him and with Colonel Siber. Siber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did the situation change any after your protest?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding the PTT building, the situation changed as of October maybe. These vehicles stopped coming to the PTT building. However, these vehicles continued moving and droving around and taking some posts next to some humanitarian facilities such as the hospital, and we used to receive too many protests in this regard, and we used to convey our opinion in this relevant manner -- matter to the officials that I have mentioned, and we vehemently reported that. I think the Secretary-General, Mr. Goulding and Mr. Morillon saw and witnessed the effect of shelling on these humanitarian facilities. They also complained to the Bosnians for the location -- for the positioning of some military forces next to these facilities. I remember the answer from Mr. Ejub Ganic. He used to tell me, Where should we go? We are fighting close to the city. I told him, You have to go. You are creating lots of problems. And if I were on the other side I would have retaliated to any firing, to any shelling, and this is a problem. I hope that I answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, General. The concentration of weapons that you spoke of yesterday during your examination, this concentration that existed in Sarajevo and also these mobile vehicles, was all of that a threat to the civilian population in Sarajevo itself?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course the presence of any military force inside residential areas constitute a threat to civilians. This is natural.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, sir, now I'd like to move on to the 28th -- the 29th of August, actually, and a meeting that was held in Sarajevo, but before that let me ask you something: The name of General Hosen, is that familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up in e-court 1D327, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I would like you to focus on -- actually -- all right. Perhaps we won't be dealing with this document a great deal, because you said that you did not know General Hosen. Do you see what it says in brackets here, that General Hosen is present with two others, and the Muslim delegation is represented by Mr. Cikotic and Siber. Out of these two attendees, are you perhaps one of them? If you look at the content of the meeting, would that perhaps jog your memory?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is obviously a minutes of a meeting that took place. You're talking about General Hosen. Hosen is not familiar to me. Maybe Husein, maybe. That's my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Sir, if that is correct, I'm sorry to say that I have a translation of the original, and I'm really reading correctly. It says "General Hosen."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, what the witness says is he at least allows for the possibility that it is an error in the transcript, and since the first name of this witness is Husein, that it may be a reference to him. And to be quite honest, that is the first thing that came to my mind as well when I read it, but ... Did you attend a meeting with, on the 29th of August, 1992, a kind of a meeting which we find in this minutes on the talks between the representative of UNPROFOR and the representative of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the presence of -- where -- and is there any chance that you arrived late?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir. Yes. I remember this meeting, and I remember Mr. Siber. At the beginning, he was not very friendly, at the beginning of this meeting, and he reminded me that I arrived five minutes late, and I apologised to that. I do remember that meeting. I told him it was out of my control, because the guide took us to another location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, the witness is present at the meeting. The only inconsistency still is that the minutes say that you were 45 minutes late, whereas the witness says he was five minutes late, but let's not focus on that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really do apologise to the witness for this misrepresentation, but in both versions, in Serbian and in English, it says General Hosen. I suppose it's a misspelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That has been established by now in detail over the last couple of minutes. Let's proceed, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Sir, if we look at what you are saying, which is somewhere in the middle of the page, and if we compare it to paragraph 77 of your statement, we can see that you are talking about the same subject. However, a little bit above that paragraph, in the middle, it says: "Three French soldiers were seriously wounded today in Nedzarici." In paragraph 78, you say that in the incident that happened in the vicinity of Butmir, two French soldiers were killed. What I am interested in is to hear from you were those two separate isolated incidents, or was there some confusion there?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: During these meetings, we used to discuss a lot of topics, and I do not recall the details of every meeting right now. You are asking me to remember that meeting in particular. The words are -- the font is very small; I cannot read very well. But these meetings in general -- during these meetings, we used to discuss similar issues, including the issue of the vehicles that were used for selling from the vicinity of the UN building. We also discussed the casualties that we incurred as a result of fighting between the two sides, and I used to encourage both sides to avoid -- to avoid shelling the UN buildings and UN locations. These were things that we discussed at most of the meetings that we held, not just that meeting in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Very well. Very well, sir. Thank you for your answer. In paragraph 74, you speak about sniping of civilian targets in Sarajevo, as well as UN facilities. Now, let's leave UN facilities aside for a moment, and I would like to draw your attention to civilian targets. When you talk about civilian targets, did you refer -- so I withdraw my question. When you speak about sniping of civilian targets, did you mean the sniping targeting civilian population?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, this is what I mean. We received reports from observers, and we noticed that a lot of casualties, a lot of the people wounded by the sniping, were children and women, and they were older people. It is as if there was a focus on these people. And if you go back to the reports that we received from the observers, you will find all these details. What interested me as well is that there were areas that were known to be sniping areas such as the area near the Holiday Inn. There was also an area behind the PTT building where a woman was killed, as I mentioned or as it was mentioned in the reports during the visit of Mr. Vance and Mr. Owen to the sector. So there was a lot of sniping targeting civilian populations in certain areas. And in those areas, when we passed through these areas, we all used to run and speed up to pass quickly through these areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know that in certain parts on the outskirts of the city of Sarajevo, the lines between the Serb and Muslim forces were only about a hundred metres apart?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Would you allow for a possibility that the victims, unfortunately those who were either killed or wounded, could have been hit from ordinary infantry weapons?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We consider these to be sniping operations when they target civilian populations. As for regular fighting and clashes between forces, this is something normal in times of war. What interested us was the operations targeting the civilians during their movement inside the city and not at the outskirts of the city. At the outskirts of the city there are very close positions, but what interested us and what pained us was to notice that there was a lot of civilian casualties as a result of sniping operations, and what I mean by sniping are individuals, men who carry weapons. They are snipers, and they target directly civilians through sniping. And you know very well what I mean by sniping. It is sniping at a civilian individual crossing a certain area. This is what we mean by sniping. As for clashes between the two sides, this is normal in times of war, and this is something that we understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying, sir. Thank you. From the city centre of Sarajevo where a tram line runs all the way to the first Serb positions, can you tell us the distance between the two?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In question direction, Mr. Petrusic? I have 360 degrees around, so therefore the question's -- or would you say wherever on this circle would be the forces closest to the town centre? Now then you have another problem, because the town centre stretches for, well, let's say one kilometre or more. So from one part of the town centre, closest may be one position, whereas from another part of the town centre it may be another -- it may be another position. So please put a question which is clear enough to get a clear answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with the -- the part of Sarajevo town which is next to the bank, and next to it is the famous historical building known as Vijecnica or town hall?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My memory, sir, does not serve me well. I do not recall all these details. I'm talking about things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Petrusic, let me interrupt. I do understand that you want to establish the distance between the confrontation line and a certain part of the city. Now, we have -- first of all, you have not told us at what point in time, because the lines moved slightly now and then. I think that there is quite some documentary evidence on confrontation lines, and even if it would not be within a margin of 50 or 60 metres but -- but -- I think there is -- at least in the binder of maps we find information about that. Why not ask Mr. Vanderpuye whether he would agree that from this building to that point where the map show that there was positions or choose whatever position you want, the distance was not more than a certain number of kilometres or metres or hundreds of metres? That is by far better than to rely on distances which necessarily are at the best a guess, unless the witness, of course, would have measured them in detail. Mr. Petrusic -- Mr. Vanderpuye, would you be willing to look at a map together with Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, I would like now to move to a meeting that you had on the 26th of October. And for that we need document 1D335, please. You can see the participants in the meeting where you yourself are present representing UNPROFOR delegation, and on behalf of delegation of the Army of Republika Srpska was General Milan Gvero. Was that your first meeting with Mr. Gvero?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as far as I recall, this meeting was the beginning of a series of meetings for the Military Committee at the airport. This is something that we suggested, myself and General Morillon -- or General Morillon made that suggestion and I encouraged it. We decided to meet with the high commanders, with the people in charge. Sometimes we were meeting with second-rank officials and that was a waste of time. So we decided that maybe if we can meet with the high commanders we could reach better results. I think that was the first of a series of meetings that took place at the airport and what we called the joint military committee meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please have page 3 in English and also page 3 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Please look at your contribution to this meeting, sir, but when you talk about freedom of movement, you were actually referring to the freedom of movement of the citizens of Sarajevo. Did that also involve the freedom of choice for the citizens of Sarajevo to either leave or come to live in the city of Sarajevo depending on their wishes?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this context, I meant the freedom of movement of UN personnel. We were suffering a lot from the closures, from the blockades, and from the -- from stopping the UN convoys and humanitarian convoys. I was talking in this meeting in my capacity as UN commander. I was finding lots of problems and difficulties in performing my duties because of closures of roads and also because of stopping UN convoys and vehicles as well as the insistence of some check-points to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Abdel-Razek, the question simply was whether you referred to the freedom of movement of the civilian population as well. The answer clearly is no. And then you start explaining why you raised the matter for the UN personnel, but the question was focused on UN personnel or civilian population. The answer seems to be clear you were talking about UN personnel, not civilian population. Please proceed, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If we look at page 6 in B/C/S and page 8, the last paragraph, in English -- or, rather, the penultimate one, you can see that General Gvero was asking for permission for 60.000 Serbs being held there to be able to leave. Was your impression that General Morillon agreed with this?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not have this impression. This is one of the requests that was reiterated during our meetings with the Serbian side, but the United Nations did not have a say or an answer, because this would mean that the United Nations were taking part in ethnic cleansing operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Sir, had information ever reached you to the effect that a large number of Serb civilians were living in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you also receive information that their desire was to leave Sarajevo and to go to a territory under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In smaller numbers, but the majority of the people I met wanted to end the situation. They wanted to co-exist, and they did not have a problem in living in Sarajevo. However, a few of them, and given the deterioration of the situation in the areas where they were living, they used to come to the PTT building seeking refuge and safe haven, then they used to return to their neighbourhood. We did not encourage such movements based on the movement of civilians based on their ethnic affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: At this meeting, did you discuss the issue of demilitarisation of the airport? Sorry, I meant to say demilitarisation of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed it. We discussed this matter, and we said -- we said that clearly during this meeting, and General Morillon explained that clearly he said that arms should be under control, and we will try to draft a cease-fire agreement, and based on this agreement, we will seek to sign it during our next meeting, and we asked all the people attending this meeting to invite to the next meeting all the military commanders, and I think that in the following meeting General Mladic was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Prior to this meeting that was held on the 26th of October, had the Serbian side before that meeting and at the request of UNPROFOR accept the proposal on demilitarisation which involved an area about 1.000 metres around the airport?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember this. What I remember is that both sides were keen to achieve demilitarisation on a consensual basis; i.e., that it happens at the same time and based on an agreement supervised by the UNPROFOR in some areas where intensive clashes were taking place and where many violations also were taking place. So demilitarisation was limited to rhetorics, because the coming days proved that it was nothing but rhetorics, and there was no genuine will on the ground to implement it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, in view of the limitations in time we have today, I suggest that we take a little bit longer first session, let's say approximately 75 minutes, that we take a little bit of a longer break, that is from quarter to 11.00 to quarter past 11.00, and then have another 75 minutes until the next break. If that does meet any objections, then I suggest that you continue for another 17 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, when you arrived in Sarajevo, did you know that the airport at the initial stage of the conflict and before the arrival of UNPROFOR had been under the control of the forces of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All what I know, sir, is that there was an agreement that was reached according to which UNPROFOR would be in charge of protecting and managing the airport, as well as ensuring operations through this airport for humanitarian convoys and reliefs. When I went to Sarajevo, this is the agreement that was enforced, and as I said in my testimony yesterday, Mr. Goulding told me that the activities in the airport were suspended for security reasons, but it was about to resume its activity and to re-open soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Abdel-Razek, again you were asked whether you knew that the airport was under the control of the Republika Srpska forces before. You told us what you know, but that is not what was there before. So, therefore, if you had said, No, I don't know. I only know what I found when I arrived, that would have done and that would be it. You see the point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir. Before arriving to Sarajevo, I did not know under whose control was the airport placed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be the direct and very simple answer to a clear question. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Apart from UNPROFOR members, was any party participating in this armed conflict, or civilians for that matter, allowed to move on the airport premises, including the runways? Was anyone else allowed access to these facilities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, in fact or under the agreement? What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am referring to the agreement as well as the factual situation in the field. I was interested in whether the witness has any direct knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you should ask two questions, one under the agreement and one whether that was respected or not, because it's unclear the way you put it. Could you tell us whether under the agreement whether any party to the armed conflict or civilians were allowed to move on the airport premises, including runways, under the agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The agreement, sir, was very clear, according to me, the airport is under the supervision of UNPROFOR. UNPROFOR would manage technically the airport for humanitarian purposes, relief purposes, as well as receiving the delegations of peacekeeping missions, as well as facilitating the movement of Bosnian officials to attend peace negotiations outside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again I urge you to -- not to say what the agreement was for but whether under the agreement or in the agreement anything is found which prohibits the warring parties or civilians to move on the premises of the airport.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was prohibited for civilians to use the airport or to move around and inside the airport because it was under the protection of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for the armed forces of the two parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No one was allowed to be present on in the runways or in the airport facilities. We only had liaison officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, now about the facts, I take it. I leave it in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If no one was allowed there, did you have information that there was movement nonetheless by civilians as well as uniformed personnel on the runways and inside the airport itself?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. I did not get your question. UNPROFOR forces were present there. Airport is under our mission. We used to go there to unload the planes with loads of relief, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, the question is: Despite that it was prohibited, did it happen or did you receive information that civilians would be on the runways or inside the airport? That's the first part of the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Your Honour. I would like to clarify this issue. No civilian was allowed to be present inside the airport except the liaison officers. However, the technical management and administration of the airport was at the hands of the UNPROFOR. So the civilians who were there were working for UNPROFOR, but not civilians who were residents of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Abdel-Razek, the question of Mr. Petrusic hints at the possibility that civilians were illegally present on the runways or in the airport premises. Did you ever receive information about civilians without permission being there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This happened when some civilians from Butmir started to cross through the runways inside the city. This is the single incident where it happened. And we warned against what happened, and there are relevant reports about this incident. However, some civilians, and they know it, I don't mean it by saying civilians from Bosnia, but civilians coming from Zagreb or other areas, because these civilians were engaged in negotiations with the relevant parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Were there persons in uniform who also used the runways or other airport facilities illegally? And I have in mind such persons who were not allowed presence there legally.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, people in uniform? I would like to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Petrusic hints at persons in military uniforms, Mr. Petrusic, illegally moving on the runways or in the airport premises.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is the question, all I remember is that there were civilians that used to cross the airport, and that was one of the issues discussed with the Bosnian side and with General Galic. And General Galic used to assure us that they were wearing military uniform, but our sources told us that they were civilians wearing civilian clothing. This is what happened regarding the movement of individuals on the runway, individuals specifically from Butmir to the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Very well, General. Let us move on to another topic, then, which you discuss in paragraphs 28 and 58 of your statement. It has to do with General Mladic. During your testimony this morning, you said you saw him for the first time after the 26th of October in 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking about General Gvero and not General Mladic. I've met General Mladic before that date, and I remember that there was a meeting with Mr. Karadzic. He attended that meeting, and I was with Mr. Morillon. But what I was mentioning this morning is that I met General Gvero after that date, and he was the head of the delegation, the Serbian -- Serbian Bosnian delegation in the joint negotiations and discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you refer to that meeting of yours, was that the meeting where in addition to General Morillon and yourself, there was also Mr. Owen who was present?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. There was another meeting when Mr. Morillon decided to have a -- a headquarters in Sarajevo Sector. We went to Ilidza and we went on a reke mission in Kiseljak, and we chose Kiseljak to be the headquarters in Bosna -- Bosnia, and of course that was in co-ordination with the high commanders. This is when we went and met with Mr. Karadzic and with General Mladic. And I think I have given a picture of that meeting to Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: During your mandate, can you tell us perhaps how many times you met with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was around four to five times.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was it always on such occasions where Republika Srpska delegations were present comprising civilians and military personnel?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On some of these occasions, yes, such as the meeting that I was referring to that was attended by Mr. Owen. There were civilians and military personnel representing Republika Srpska, and there was Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Lukic, and Dr. Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, I'm looking at the clock. I suggest that we take a break of half an hour now, a little bit of a longer break. But first, Mr. Abdel-Razek, would you please follow the usher. We would like to see you back in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, the estimate you gave yesterday is still valid?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means some time would be left for Mr. Vanderpuye to re-examine the witness. We take a break, and we resume at quarter past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Vanderpuye, as matters stand now, how much time you think you'd need for re-examination so that Mr. Petrusic could consider to what extent he can accommodate you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I think not more than five or ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five or ten minutes, Mr. Petrusic. Because there's another reason why the Chamber very much would like to conclude the testimony of this witness today. The Arabic interpreters are not available next week. They're only available on the 18th of October, which is a non-sitting week, just -- yes, after the 18th of October. So that means that we could not continue until early November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Abdel-Razek. Mr. Petrusic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, following the London Conference, which took place in September 1992, as you say, you had a meeting with President Karadzic, who flatly refused your request that artillery be placed under UN control. Further below in paragraph 28, you say that he could not have made that decision without Mladic's approval. My first question is this: Did you know that President Karadzic was also the supreme commander of the armed forces of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know his title. I knew that he was the head of the SDS, and this is how I was dealing with him. This is the title that we knew at the United Nations. However, his presidential title, this is something that I was not aware of. It was not in the correspondence of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If Radovan Karadzic was the supreme commander, and he indeed was, I believe that is not in dispute, would you agree with me then that General Mladic, as the commander of the armed forces of Republika Srpska, was his subordinate?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, and I also understand that the military decisions must be taken in consultation with the military advisors, with the military leaders in any country, because the political leader, when he takes a decision related to military issues, he must consult with his assistants, with his -- with the people working with him. That's normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did know that Radovan Karadzic, as the supreme commander of the armed forces, had his ministry of the military, which was headed by a general, a military man whom Mr. Karadzic could consult on military issues?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no objection to that. I understand that completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: At the aforementioned meeting when Karadzic flatly refused to make such decision, there was no one else in attendance save for yourself and Mr. Karadzic, of course -- or let me put it this way: Was there anyone from the top brass of the armed forces of Republika Srpska, anyone from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, General Mladic was not present -- present at that meeting. I hope I remember well, and I think that Mr. Krajisnik was present, but he was in an official capacity with Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So you have no tangible evidence save for your opinion or presumption that such decision was approved by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I said in my first statement that it was my personal impression, and if you may allow me to clarify this. In the military statements made by Mr. Karadzic following the London Conference and all the correspondence between Goulding and Mr. Nambiar and everything I learned from Mr. Nambiar when I first met with him, I understood that Mr. Karadzic committed to gathering the weapons and putting them under the UN control. Furthermore, he also agreed to withdraw from certain areas, sensitive areas, in order to reduce the tension and reduce the escalation in the situation. This is why when I met him a second time and he told me something contrary to what I already heard --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, excuse me for interrupting. You have expanded on that in your statement as well as in your previous answer. I'm content with that. Therefore, we could move on. I wanted to apologise once again for having interrupted you. Let us move on. Did you personally at those meetings you attended with General Mladic express or table certain problems regarding Sarajevo and, if so, can you tell us when those meetings took place and which delegations were present?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never mentioned meeting General Mladic personally, and we discussed specific issues. Most of my meetings took place with Mr. Galic, but when the UN delegation met Mr. Karadzic, usually Mr. Mladic was present at most of these meetings. The only meeting that took place between myself -- or the only discussions that took place were friendly discussions mainly on the occasion of Christmas. We talked about general things, and I think that he asked me at the time to go back and tell the Egyptian authorities to send a military attache to this Republika Srpska, and I told him that I was not authorised to do that. So it was a friendly conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Abdel-Razek, Mr. Petrusic is referring to all the meetings you had where General Mladic was present. Did you raise any problems during such meetings, and do you remember at what meeting you raised what problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the meetings of the joint military commission at the airport, I spoke in my capacity as UN commander in Sarajevo. I raised the problems. He was there, and he agreed on the signing of the cease-fire agreement which was supposed to take place during that meeting, but this did not take place, did not happen. During that meeting, everyone was raising the problems he was facing, and I also raised the problems we were facing in the Sarajevo Sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you briefly list, not explain but just list the problems you raised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problems I raised were the following: Continuous shelling; the blockade of UN convoys and of humanitarian convoys; I also mentioned the problems we were facing with the Presidency side when it comes to humanitarian matters. We were required to ensure the provision of fuel, to provide generators for the hospitals, et cetera. I was mentioning and raising all these problems in such meetings. There was also another important topic which was the disappearance of the three civilian drivers who were evacuating the students who were stuck in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One additional question. From this list, do I understand that you did not raise any sniping problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned shelling. When I say "shelling," I meant also -- it also comprises sniping and any other military activity targeting civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask for 1D343 which is relating to this topic. I have to tell you that we have a draft translation into English which was done by somebody from our office; hence this document could only be marked for identification, and we will be tendering it as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, in the introduction of this document issued by Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic on the 11th of November, 1992, it reads: "On the basis of an agreement on the unconditional cessation of hostilities in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina," and the agreement in question had to do with both Serb and Muslim forces. It is ordered to implement the following conduct, and then on page 2 in item 2 of the English version we see that the "kag" acronym should stand for "corps artillery group" and that such firing cannot be executed without the approval of the commander of the Main Staff. This order was forwarded inter alia to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. The corps had the area of responsibility which included the city of Sarajevo. My question is this: Does this order reflect the contents of the meeting as discussed at the airport by you and General Mladic as well as the rest of the delegation?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, sir. And based on this order -- sorry. I knew from General Galic that he issued an order to his subordinates. However, unfortunately, the situation did not prevail for a long period of time, and firing and shelling continues for a long period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I seek clarification of the answer. You said: "I knew from General Galic that he issued an order to his subordinates." Do you mean to say that General Galic issued an order to his subordinates, or did you mean to say that General Mladic issued an order to his subordinates, because we are looking at an order apparently issued by General Mladic? Which of the two you meant when you said "he issued an order"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what happens in military matters. Orders are issued from the commanders to the commanders of sectors, and then the commanders of the sectors issue orders to the various units. So if Galic told me that there is an order in this regard, this means that this order was issued based on instructions from General Mladic. This is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Since you've already mentioned General Galic, I would also like to ask for a document, P302.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I do apologise. Should I tender the documents as I deal with them, or should I tender them all together at the end of the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can tender them once you're dealing with them. Did you want to tender the previous document, the order which we have on our screen now?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it you want to have it marked for identification because there is no final translation yet. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D343 becomes Exhibit D65 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And keeps that status for the time being. Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have the next document now, and that is -- yes. Yes. Yes, it's already on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 10th of October, 1992. It was issued by the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and it was signed by the commander, Stanislav Galic. General, sir, you will see paragraphs 1 and 2 that have to do with the ban on using any kind of artillery weaponry and also the ban on opening any kind of fire at the town of Sarajevo. Will you agree with me that General Galic issued this order on the basis of the order of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska as is stated at the end of this document that we have here?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Further on does that mean that the order of the Main Staff that General Galic received could not have been changed by him?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, sir. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would also like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar. It's already in evidence because it was called as --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, when you came to Sarajevo, when you started your tour there, as you journeyed from the airport to your command, you noticed some damage on the buildings there, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Just after you took -- took up your command duty, you had a meeting with General Galic?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic was present as well, wasn't she?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did General Galic present to you the position of his superior command, the Main Staff, that is, in relation to Sarajevo? That is to say both in terms of shelling and sniping.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We apologise, but we could not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear your answer. Could you please repeat the start of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During that meeting, I was introducing myself to the various relevant stakeholders, and this meeting was mostly an introductory meeting, and I was seeking their co-operation in order to achieve the success of the UNPROFOR mission in the sector. However, we did not tackle too many details during that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But was the position of the superior command discussed in relation to shelling and sniping in relation to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, sir. It was an introductory meeting. I was introducing myself to the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you, General. 1D336. Could I now have that document, please. It is a fact that this document was issued a month before you arrived. However, do allow me just briefly to focus on this document with you. The 13th of July, 1992, is the date, and it is signed by General Ratko Mladic. It is a document of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. General, would you please focus on page 2. Of course you can look at page 1 as well; the first paragraph, that is. Once you've had a look, could you please tell me so that we can have the second page displayed for you.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Could you please [indiscernible]. I can't catch the word. Yes. Thank you. Thank you. Okay. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the second page of the document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I'd like to draw your attention to -- yes, well, the only paragraph, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see orders issued by a higher command to the relevant commands in the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, in relation to the previous orders that you saw, October and November, this document that was issued on the 13th of July, does it differ in any way -- sorry. General Mladic, who issued this document, is he fully consistent in terms of not allowing shelling and not allowing the use of artillery against the town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, isn't it true that the consistency or inconsistency between documentary evidence is for the Chamber to decide? Of course, unless the witness sees anything very special, but this is a document which deals with matters before his arrival, and you're more or less asking the witness to interpret the document. Again, if he has any specific knowledge on specific matters appearing in this document, it may be of some use. Otherwise, I don't see what use it serves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: These three documents, are they consistent, the three documents that you had an opportunity to see?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently you do not understand my comment, Mr. Petrusic. Would you please put your next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the further talks that you had, did General Galic suggest to you -- or, rather, did he ever say to you that he had had explicit orders from his superior command not to use artillery weapons in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I mentioned. He said that there are orders, that he issued orders, and I told him that these orders should be communicated to your staff and that you should ensure that it is followed up. And he confirmed it, and this means that he received orders from the higher command. We say instructions are issued by the higher command and orders are issued to the subordinates. This is the terminology we use.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D336 becomes Exhibit D66, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, do you know what General Galic's attitude was towards his superior command?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Specifically I don't know such things. I'm not aware of them. But when I talked about his relations with his superior command, I was talking about my personal impression, and I reiterated that several times. We are generals who understand how things happen, and I was talking about a personal impression here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could anyone else issued orders to General Galic?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir. I don't know. All I know concerning that specific issues is that he said there were directives, and I have given my instructions to my subordinates but I do not know what is the relationship between the military and the political commands, how orders are received from whom. I don't know all these details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, before you move to the next -- to your next question, the document which was admitted a second ago, D66, may I take it that the translation originates from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at -- only at the stamp where it mentions the 4th of June, where I see some handwriting which is 1407 rather than the 4th of June. I don't see anything of the kind. So could perhaps the translation be verified. I recognise the 204 on the second line, but the 4th of June, the only thing I see is 1407 in handwriting, or if the 1 is not a 1 but just a dash, then it would still be the 4th of July rather than the 4th of June. So I have difficulties in accepting this to be an accurate translation. Could you please check that, Mr. Vanderpuye, and if need be, inform Mr. Petrusic. Meanwhile, Mr. Petrusic may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document 1D347, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This is also a draft translation from the Office of the Defence. General, would you please familiarise yourself with the content of this document, and then please tell us whether you recall this situation.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I have to have the camera to be focused on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. I was just going to indicate that we perhaps could blow it up so he could see a little better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I -- I remember this, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In spite of the order issued by General Mladic last Tuesday which refers to the removal of a container and wooden obstacles on the road leading to the airport, these obstacles and this container are still in the same place. Is this an order that you received from General Mladic, and, actually, how did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This order is clear. We at the UN, we communicate with people at the various levels, at the command level, the field level, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll stop you again, Mr. Abdel-Razek. The question is how were you aware of this order having been issued by Mr. Mladic. Did you hear it? Did you see it? If you heard it, from whom did you hear it? If you saw it, how did you obtain the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is linked to the first meeting that I had with General Galic during which he told me that there were directive issued, and usually when he received directives from General Mladic he issues instructions. This is how I understand things from a military perspective. When there is a directive issued from the higher command, the commander issues instructions to his subordinates. So I was referring to the instructions given by the general, and despite these instructions the situation did not get better. This is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the answer is you heard of such an order when you met with General Galic. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: After your intervention did the situation improve, specifically in this case?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that I met with Galic a second time, and we reached an agreement that the container or the obstacles that were placed along the airport road, he was worried that the other side will be using the airport. So I told him we will supervise the control of the airport by opening up another route. We agreed on that, and on the following day this was executed. And I issued orders to the French battalion asking them to put a control point along the airport road in order to prevent any obstacles to the UN vehicles and the UN convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a draft translation, yes, a draft translation, and I would like to tender this document for identification purposes only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D347 becomes Exhibit D67 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. It keeps that status for a while. Mr. Vanderpuye, if finally a -- if a final translation will have been received, would there be any objection as far as you can see now?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, during your mandate, did you receive any protests or complaints from the Serbian side to the effect that UNPROFOR members and members of other international organisations were smuggling in weapons for the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I never heard such objections. They were never raised in my meetings with anyone. I've never heard about the smuggling of weapons by UNPROFOR forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: How about other international organisations?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never heard of that either. Throughout my presence in Sarajevo, I've never heard that other international organisations were smuggling weapons to the Bosnian government forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have a document -- or, rather, a video-clip, 1D358. The transcript of the interpretation was produced by the Defence office.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: The booths don't have the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The booth complains -- or at least states they have no transcript, Mr. Petrusic. Apparently not in either language.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it lasts for about one minute. Can we play it without the sound, and possibly ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And possibly what, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that possibly we could see members of the peacekeeping forces, and I would like to ask the general if he can recognise certain soldiers in this video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If a party does not rely on the sound and any words spoken, then the video may be played without sound, and it has to be played only once. Please play the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, in this video were you able to recognise anything?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In reality, the video does not show where did that happen and the exact situation. We see a number of images, but that's not something I've heard about neither through complaints or protests from the command, and I really don't know where that happened and what are the details of the situation. That's not something I've heard about. That's not something I was informed about. There were no official communications about that. However, there was smuggling of fuel, but this is another story. It was a disciplinary issue. There was smuggling of fuel from the Ukrainian battalion. They were selling fuel outside of Sarajevo, and we investigated that with the police, and measures were taken against the violators. There were other incidents. For example, they took a car. They stole a car. But there was a investigation with the police, and I issued a suggestion for the head of that battalion to be sent back to his home country, but that was a different matter, a disciplinary matter. Concerning this, I haven't heard anything about this. I have no information. And I would like to add something if it's possible. As a military man, I know that these things happen in times of war. Nobody can control everything that's going on on the ground, nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But, sir, in any case, you were able to recognise blue helmets in this video, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UN can investigate the matter, and if I recall well, there is someone that I might have recognised. It's Major Jackson. He was Canadian, and he used to work with us in operations, but this is someone that I do not doubt at all. I don't doubt at all his discipline. I don't think that he has anything to do with that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you recognise any other person apart from the person you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I was trying to focus on the blue helmets. They seem to be soldiers, and it would be difficult for me to remember, but the person wearing glasses, I think he was a major, if I recall well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it from your answers that you did not recognise the location where this was filmed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Interpretation] ... I could see a container and this is the container I was referring to. It was in the middle of the road between Otes and the airport. And -- and we put that container instead of the container that was placed previously by the Serbian forces in order to control access to the airport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Petrusic. And keep in mind that we are coming closer and closer to the point in time where Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am at the very end, perhaps one or two more questions, but before that, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, any --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Referring to the video-tape in terms of doc'ing it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would ask that it be marked for identification at this point. I don't know what it says, and it may, in fact, support or not support what the witness has said about it or what counsel's representations are as to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, just looking at all this, the probative value is entirely unclear to the Chamber. Apparently you also have -- you cannot rely on it because what the witness says is not -- is not anyway -- in any way support what may be your interpretation of this video of which the Chamber is not aware yet. Therefore, admission is denied without prejudice. If at any later stage you consider that it could be tendered again, then we'll look at it at that moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware or did you have any information at all that sometime in early January 1993, the Muslim forces started digging a tunnel underneath the airport runway in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I've never heard of such thing. All I've heard is that there were civilians crossing the runway from Butmir to the city and vice versa. And this is something that was mentioned in my statement. As for a tunnel, I've never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Sir, you spoke about the shelling of a funeral procession, and in your statement, you indicate that fire came from the Serbian side. Would you allow for a possibility that there could be other interpretations and other perceptions in the sense that perhaps the other party, that is to say the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, were the ones who opened fire at this funeral procession in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were lots of allegations from the various parties, and the Serbian side often said that the Bosnian side was opening fire on civilians and on buildings in order to get the sympathy from the international community and to get international support. This is something that we heard often in all meetings. Every party tried to distance itself from these allegations, said they were not committing these mistakes and these violations. This is all I know. There were allegations from both sides, but the Serbian side often said that the other side was doing that to -- to themselves in order to justify an international intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, thank you. I have no further questions for you. Your Honours, this concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you would need anything between five and ten minutes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, I just have a few questions for you. At page 7 of today's transcript -- are you all right?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yeah. Yeah. Yes. Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At page 7 of today's transcript you were asked a number of questions concerning what you had referred to about retaliation in respect of fire that was drawn from mobile units, and in particular, I wondered if you had ever spoken to General Galic about this retaliation or this retaliatory fire while you were in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir. It was very clear. I told him, You are firing at the UN building, and you should understand what the consequences will be. We turned into victims similar to the civilians in Sarajevo. We are targeted by fire, shelling, mortar bombs. He said, Fires were coming -- fire was coming from your direction. I told him, Yes, I know. I protested strongly, and I told the other side very strongly that this should stop and no vehicles should -- no vehicles should fire from within a perimeter of 500 metres from UN premises according to UN rules. And he -- he said, Should they stop firing, we will also act in the same way and stop retaliating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, the answer to your question is found, I have here unnumbered, page 15 of the statement, last paragraph there. Seventy-seven. So, therefore, what is in the statement doesn't need to be further asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm not asking about the statement. I'm asking about his statement regarding it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but your question was whether he ever discussed it with General Galic. That was your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, it's clear from this paragraph that "I recall one meeting prior to my last meeting with General Galic. He told me --" so he discussed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recall what you said in your testimony in the Karadzic case about your talk with General Galic on this matter? If you don't, I'll be happy to read a little bit of it to you to refresh your recollection.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What you said in the Karadzic case, and this is 20 July 2010 with respect to this conversation, is that you told General Galic: "You should not retaliate --" and by the way this is at page 5554 of the transcript. You told General Galic that: "I will accept that there are forces that are positioned in certain places, but you should be wise. You should not retaliate against areas where there are many civilians. You should not retaliate against areas where there are -- you can retaliate," rather, "somewhere else along the front, but to attack areas where there are civilians, this is a mistake. It brings major injuries. It hurts us. It hurts public opinion, because in brief there are civilians getting killed, and there are humanitarian facilities and hospitals that are getting destroyed and unable to function. So they should move away from shelling any civilian population centres." Does that sound about right?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir, I said that I was getting into details because I was provided with details, and this is what I said exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked at today's transcript, I think it's page 34, if anyone could issue General Galic orders, or anyone else could issue General Galic orders, and you said that you didn't know. You did say at your statement, however, that General Galic received orders to conduct shooting and shelling. You believe he followed them because he was a soldier. This is at paragraph 121. To your knowledge and understanding during the time you were in Sarajevo, who was General Galic's commander?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN ALY ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I clearly said that this was my personal impression. I knew the commanders. This is a personal impression. According to my impression, Galic is one of these commanders who implements the orders fully and exactly. If he receives order to proceed into shelling, he would do so. I said that this is my own impression, my own personal impression based on my meetings with him. This is what I meant, should this clarify my answer. So I suppose that he received an order, and I invite you once again to go back to the relevant documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
